hypothesis: GenAI is now material revenue, not a pilot-stage side line.
test: AI share of revenue at disclosing firms; size of the eight-firm AI pool.
evidence: TCS 10.1% and Infosys 10.5% of revenue (company-disclosed); eight-firm AI run-rate ~$15.8 bn (range $13.2-18.9 bn), ~7.6% of their combined revenue. TCS's AI run-rate rose 72% in three quarters ($1.8 bn to $3.1 bn).
so_what: AI is now big enough to move the P&L. The open question has shifted from 'is AI real?' to 'is AI net-additive?'.

hypothesis: AI revenue growth is arriving alongside a shrinking core business (AI deflation).
test: Split revenue into AI and non-AI at two points for every firm with an AI time series; annualise each.
evidence: Core (non-AI) revenue shrank at all three Indian disclosers: Infosys -5.9%/yr, TCS -3.6%/yr, HCLTech -0.5%/yr, while total revenue grew only 2.2-2.4%. Accenture's core still grew +4.7% (FY24-FY25).
verdict: Supported for TCS and Infosys: an upper bound, as TCS core rests on two data points; weaker for HCLTech; not seen at Accenture
so_what: At TCS and Infosys, AI growth is so far replacing core revenue, not adding to it. That fits the 2-3.5%/yr deflation analysts cite. Part of the shift may be existing work relabelled as AI, which no firm discloses.

hypothesis: The firms with the most AI revenue are not the ones growing fastest.
test: Spearman rank correlation between AI share of revenue and constant-currency revenue growth (8 firms; and the 4 company-based disclosers).
evidence: Rank correlation -0.05 across all eight (p=0.91) and -0.40 across the four disclosers (n=4, not testable). Five of the eight AI shares are estimates or peer benchmarks. Infosys (10.5% AI) grew 1.5%; TCS (10.1%) 2.8%; Capgemini (est. 8%) 11.7% incl. WNS; Tech Mahindra (est. 5%) 7.2%.
verdict: Supported, directionally: AI share shows no positive link to growth (n=8, not statistically significant)
so_what: 'AI revenue' is not yet a growth KPI. For CI and investor work, track core growth and book-to-bill next to the AI number.

hypothesis: AI has decoupled revenue from headcount.
test: Revenue growth minus headcount growth (YoY), and revenue per employee.
evidence: Median gap only +1.4pp. Six of eight show weak or no decoupling. Revenue per employee rose 0.5-1.7% at most firms; Tech Mahindra is the outlier (+6.9%, headcount down). Capgemini's headcount jumped 18% with the WNS acquisition.
verdict: Not yet visible: headcount still moves broadly with revenue; Tech Mahindra is the exception
so_what: Productivity gains are being passed to clients as price, not kept as margin or non-linear growth. That is the deflation mechanism in H2 seen from the people side.

hypothesis: Announcement momentum (Project 1's CI events) predicts AI monetisation.
test: Spearman rank correlation of verified Project 1 events per firm against AI share of revenue and against growth.
evidence: Rank correlations (n=8): events vs AI share -0.14 (p=0.75); events vs growth -0.57 (p=0.14, not significant). HCLTech and Cognizant lead on event count (12 each), with TCS and Wipro on 11. Wipro's revenue is flat and it discloses no AI revenue; Capgemini has no frontier-lab ties and the fastest growth (11.7% incl. WNS).
verdict: Not supported: announcement counts do not predict AI revenue or growth (n=8, not significant)
so_what: Partnership press releases are a weak lead indicator. A CI programme should weight disclosed AI revenue, core growth and bookings above announcement counts. That is the main design lesson carried back to Project 1.
